turns.user: i got a stipend of 18k a month from an internship last year and tds was cut. how do i file my itr for ay 2025-26
turns.assistant:
Steps for a salaried/stipend case:

1. Collect Form 16 (or Form 16A if it was a stipend, not salary) from the company, and check Form 26AS / AIS on the income tax portal to confirm the TDS shows up.
2. Log in at incometax.gov.in with your PAN.
3. Go to e-File > Income Tax Returns > File Income Tax Return, pick AY 2025-26, mode Online.
4. Choose status Individual, then the form. If it's salary/stipend only, ITR-1 usually works. If the company paid it as a professional fee, you'd likely need ITR-3 or ITR-4.
5. The portal pre-fills most details. Check them, add income, and claim any deductions.
6. Verify with Aadhaar OTP or net banking e-verify.

One thing to check first: was it paid as salary or as a stipend with 'professional fees' on the certificate? That decides the form.

turns.user: its form 16a, says professional fees. so itr 4?
turns.assistant:
Yes, ITR-4 (Sugam) is probably right if you want to use presumptive taxation under 44ADA, where 50% of the receipts are treated as your income. ITR-3 is for when you keep actual books and expenses.

With 18k x however many months, your total will probably be way under the basic exemption limit anyway. So the main point of filing is to claim back the TDS as a refund. Under the new regime there's no tax up to 3 lakh (4 lakh from FY 2025-26 with the revised slabs), and the 87A rebate covers more. So you'd likely get the whole TDS amount back.

turns.user: ok how do i actually do that refund part
turns.assistant:
The refund is automatic once the return is processed, you just need to set it up properly:

1. Before filing, go to Profile > My Bank Account and make sure one account is added and **validated** (pre-validated), and tick it as the refund account.
2. In the ITR, the TDS from Form 26AS/AIS gets pulled into the 'Tax Paid' schedule. Check the amount matches your Form 16A.
3. Total tax payable will come out as zero, and the TDS shows as refund due.
4. Submit, then e-verify within 30 days. If you don't verify, the return is treated as not filed.
5. Processing normally takes a few weeks, and the refund goes to your validated bank account. You'll get an email when it's processed.

turns.user: do i pick old or new regime
turns.assistant:
For a student with a small income, the new regime is almost always better. It has the higher basic exemption and the 87A rebate, and you don't have deductions like 80C or HRA that would justify the old regime anyway.

In ITR-4 you'll see a question about opting out of the new regime (the default is new). Just leave it as the default. Only switch to old if you have sizable deductions, say 80C investments, health insurance premiums or an education loan interest, that push your taxable income lower than the new regime would.

turns.user: what if i missed the july deadline
turns.assistant:
You can still file a belated return under section 139(4). For AY 2025-26 the last date for that is 31 December 2025.

Things that change:
- A late fee under section 234F: Rs 1,000 if your total income is below 5 lakh (Rs 5,000 otherwise). Since you have no tax payable and a refund due, you'd still pay this fee, but it can be adjusted against the refund.
- Interest on any unpaid tax, which is zero for you.
- You can't carry forward certain losses, which doesn't apply here.

Select 'Filed under section 139(4)' in the return filing section. The rest of the steps are identical, and the refund still comes through. If the date has gone past even this, you can file an updated return (ITR-U) with some extra tax, so it's worth sorting this soon.

turns.user: Our 5 month old lab puppy bites constantly when we play and my husband says she'll grow out of it. I'm not so sure. Why do puppies do this and does it actually go away on its own?
turns.assistant:
Mostly yes, but not entirely on its own. Puppies mouth things because it's how they explore the world and play with littermates. In a litter, when a puppy bites too hard, the other one yelps and stops playing. That feedback is how they learn to control their bite force, called bite inhibition.

At 5 months she's also teething, since adult teeth come in between about 4 and 6 months, so chewing feels good and relieves discomfort.

Most puppies do ease off as the teething ends and they mature, around 6 to 8 months. But dogs who are allowed to keep rewarded for mouthing (because it gets attention, or people keep playing when she bites) can hold onto the habit. So your husband is partly right, but she needs consistent guidance so that it fades rather than just sticks around.

turns.user: That makes sense. What do we actually do when she bites then? We've tried saying no but she just gets more excited.
turns.assistant:
That's common, and it makes sense why. For a puppy, a loud 'no', pushing her away, or flapping your hands is all attention and movement, which is exactly what an excited puppy wants more of.

What tends to work is removing the fun. When her teeth touch skin, say a calm 'ouch', stop moving, and either turn away or step out of reach for 10 to 20 seconds. Then come back and restart play. She learns that biting ends the game, and gentle play keeps it going. It works because dogs learn from what happens right after a behavior, not from the word.

Also give her something legal to bite right away, like a rope toy, and keep it in play so she has an alternative. Everyone in the house needs to do the same thing, otherwise she learns it only matters with some people.

turns.user: Thank you. One more thing, she seems to bite worst in the evening when I get home from work, is there a reason for that?
turns.assistant:
Yes, there usually is. Puppies often get a burst of wild energy in the evening, nicknamed 'the witching hour' or zoomies. It's partly because they're overtired, in the same way a toddler gets wild before bedtime, and partly because she's been alone or quiet during the day and your arrival is the most exciting moment of her day.

Overtired puppies lose self-control, so biting gets worse. What can help is a calm routine when you come in: say a quiet hello, let her settle, then give her something to chew on or a food puzzle, like a stuffed Kong, for 15 to 20 minutes. A short walk or a sniffing game beforehand also helps. If she still gets frantic, a nap in her crate or pen is often the best fix, because she may simply need to sleep.

turns.user: my lower back has been killing me for like 3 weeks, sit all day at work then chasing kids. trying to decide between physio, a chiropractor or just doing yoga on youtube. which is the best idea
turns.assistant:
For ongoing low back pain from sitting plus lifting kids, I'd rank them like this:

- **Physio**: usually the best first stop. They assess what's actually going on (tight hips, weak core, how you move) and give you specific exercises. Evidence is strong for exercise-based treatment for non-specific back pain.
- **Chiropractor**: can give short-term relief for some people, mainly from spinal manipulation, but the long-term evidence isn't better than physio. Some people like it, but it tends to mean repeat visits.
- **YouTube yoga**: free and fine for general mobility, but without knowing what's causing your pain, some poses (deep forward folds, for example) can aggravate it.

If there's no numbness, leg weakness or pain that wakes you at night, start with physio. Is the pain on one side or the middle, and does it go down your leg?

turns.user: middle mostly, sometimes a bit in the right butt cheek. no numbness
turns.assistant:
That pattern, central low back with some referral into the buttock and no numbness, is really common with muscle or joint irritation, and it's often linked to sitting a lot. It doesn't sound alarming.

That makes physio an even better fit, as they can check your hips and the joints at the base of your spine and give you targeted moves. Many physios can also see you without a doctor's referral, depending on where you live.

In the meantime, gentle walking, changing positions every 30 minutes and avoiding long periods in bed tend to help more than rest. If anything changes, like numbness, weakness, trouble with bladder or bowel, then get seen urgently.

turns.user: physio is like $120 a session tho. chiro is 60
turns.assistant:
That's a real factor. A few ways to think about it:

- Check your insurance, since many plans cover physio, sometimes chiro too, and an HSA/FSA can usually be used for both.
- With physio you may not need many visits. Often 2 to 4 sessions is enough to get a diagnosis and a home program, and then you do the work yourself.
- Chiro at $60 is cheaper per visit, but plans often involve more visits over several weeks, so the total can end up similar or higher.

If cost is the main issue, a reasonable middle path is one physio session for assessment and exercises, then do those at home, and skip a long course of either.

turns.user: ok and would yoga be bad to do in the meantime or fine
turns.assistant:
Mostly fine if you're gentle and choose well. Poses that tend to help: cat-cow, child's pose, supine knee hugs and gentle hip openers like a figure-4 stretch. Avoid anything that makes the pain sharper or sends it down the leg, and skip deep forward folds, big twists and full backbends for now.

A useful rule is that mild stretching discomfort is okay, but pain that is worse afterwards or the next morning means you overdid it. A beginner or 'yoga for back pain' video of 10 to 15 minutes is better than a full vinyasa class.

turns.user: what about a standing desk, worth buying? ive seen one for 250
turns.assistant:
It can help but isn't a cure. Research shows standing desks reduce sitting time, and some studies show a small drop in low back discomfort, but standing still for hours can cause its own aches too. The best approach is changing position often: sit for 30 to 45 minutes, stand for a bit, walk for a moment.

For $250, you could first test the idea for free by propping your laptop on a stack of books or a box for part of the day. If you actually use it for a couple of weeks, then buying makes sense. Just make sure whatever you buy is adjustable, since you want the screen at eye level and your elbows around 90 degrees.

That plan is solid. A few additions:

- Walk a bit daily, even 10 minutes a few times a day. It's one of the most reliable things for back pain.
- When lifting your kids, hold them close to your body and bend at the hips and knees, rather than twisting.
- Set a timer to get up every 30 minutes or so at work.
- A small rolled towel behind your lower back in your chair can ease the strain.

Most cases like this settle in a few weeks to a couple of months. If it's not improving in 6 weeks or it gets worse, go back to a doctor.

turns.user: can someone explain the 50/30/20 budget thing? like why those numbers. we take home about 5200 a month with 2 kids
turns.assistant:
It's a rule of thumb from Elizabeth Warren's book. You split your after-tax income into three buckets:

- 50% for needs: rent/mortgage, groceries, utilities, insurance, minimum debt payments, childcare
- 30% for wants: dining out, subscriptions, hobbies, trips
- 20% for savings and extra debt payments

The numbers aren't magic. The idea is that if needs stay around half of your income, you have room to both enjoy life and build a safety net. On $5,200, that works out to $2,600 needs, $1,560 wants and $1,040 savings.

It's a starting point, not a law. With kids and childcare, needs often go over 50%, and that's very common.

turns.user: yeah ours is more like 65% needs. is that bad
turns.assistant:
Not bad, just tight. It means the framework needs adjusting to you, not that you're doing it wrong. Housing and childcare costs in many areas make 50% unrealistic.

When needs are 65%, you have 35% left. A workable split might be something like 65/15/20 or 65/20/15. The point of the percentages is to keep the savings piece protected. Ideally, you pay yourself first, so the savings transfer happens right after payday and wants get what's left.

It's worth checking if anything in the needs bucket is actually flexible, like insurance rates, phone plans, or grocery spending, but only if it doesn't mean extra stress.

turns.user: why do people say to pay yourself first tho, whats the difference if its the same total
turns.assistant:
The total is the same on paper, but behavior is different. If you save whatever's left at the end of the month, there's often nothing left, because spending expands to fill what's available and small purchases add up without you noticing.

If you move the money out on payday into a separate savings account, you only see and spend the remainder. It's a decision made once rather than every day, so it doesn't rely on willpower. Automating it makes it even easier.

turns.user: ok makes sense. how much should the savings go to first, emergency fund or retirement or what
turns.assistant:
A common order is:

1. A small starter emergency fund first, like $1,000 to $2,000, so a car repair doesn't land on a credit card.
2. If your employer matches retirement contributions, contribute enough to get the full match, since that is free money.
3. Pay off high-interest debt (credit cards, above about 8 to 10%).
4. Build the emergency fund up to 3 to 6 months of essential expenses. With kids, I'd lean toward the higher end.
5. Then increase retirement savings, and other goals such as college.

The reasoning is that each step protects you from needing to undo the next one. Without a cushion, an emergency can force you to take on debt or withdraw from retirement accounts.

turns.user: im trying to share a little python script i wrote with my coworkers, it has 3 files and uses requests + pandas. what are my options for packaging it so they can use it easily
turns.assistant:
Some options, from simplest to most involved:

1. **Just share the folder plus requirements.txt.** They create a venv and run `pip install -r requirements.txt`. Works fine for a few people.
2. **A proper package with pyproject.toml.** They can `pip install .` or install from a git URL. Good if you want a command-line entry point.
3. **Install from a private git repo.** `pip install git+https://github.com/yourorg/yourtool.git`, which makes updating simple.
4. **Standalone executable with PyInstaller or shiv/zipapp.** Good if coworkers don't have Python at all.
5. **Internal package index.** Overkill unless you have many tools.

What do your coworkers use, and do they know Python or just need to run it?

turns.user: mostly not technical, they just want to run it. windows machines
turns.assistant:
Then the best candidate is a standalone executable.

- **PyInstaller**: `pyinstaller --onefile yourscript.py` produces an .exe they can double-click. With pandas the file can be 50 to 100+ MB, but it works. You'd need to build on a Windows machine.
- **Briefcase or Nuitka**: alternatives, but they're more involved.

If they'll only run it a few times, another option is to ship a small `run.bat` that creates a venv and installs the requirements on first run. That needs Python to be installed on their machines, though.

One warning: antivirus tools on corporate Windows sometimes flag PyInstaller exes as suspicious, so test with IT in advance.

turns.user: hmm the antivirus thing worries me. anything else
turns.assistant:
A few other routes that avoid that:

- **Shared network drive with a bundled Python.** Use the embeddable Python distribution from python.org, put your script and the packages in the same folder, and add a .bat launcher. No install and no exe to flag.
- **Turn it into a small web app.** Use Streamlit or Flask on one internal machine and coworkers just open a URL. No installs on their side at all.
- **Get IT to sign or whitelist the PyInstaller exe.** A code-signing cert helps if your company has one.
- **Use a Jupyter notebook or Excel front end,** if they live in Excel, such as xlwings.

The internal web app is often the least trouble for non-technical users, if the script's inputs and outputs are simple.

turns.user: the streamlit idea sounds good. is that hard to set up
turns.assistant:
Not hard if the script already does the work in functions. The basic path:

1. `pip install streamlit` in a venv on the machine that will host it.
2. Make an `app.py` that imports your code and adds a few widgets, e.g. `st.file_uploader`, `st.button('Run')`, and `st.dataframe(result)` to show the output.
3. Run `streamlit run app.py`. It starts on port 8501.
4. Coworkers open `http://machine-name:8501` in a browser.

The annoying parts are keeping it running (use a scheduled task, NSSM, or a Docker container) and access, since you should make sure it's only reachable on your internal network. For a handful of coworkers, it's usually an afternoon of work.
